content: 1. The effective use of a diagnostic algorithm with adequate sensitivity and specificity is essential for diagnosing tuberculosis (TB). 2. Individuals who use drugs are those who engage in harmful or hazardous use of psychoactive substances, which can negatively affect their health, social life, resources, or legal situation. 3. Presumptive tuberculosis refers to individuals presenting with symptoms or signs suggestive of TB. 4. Previously treated individuals are those who have received at least one month or more of TB medications in the past. These individuals may have been treated with a first-line regimen for drug-susceptible TB or a second-line regimen for drug-resistant TB. 5. Programmatic management of TB preventive treatment involves all coordinated activities by public and private healthcare providers and the community to scale up TB preventive treatment for those in need. 6. Miliary TB is classified as pulmonary TB (PTB) because it involves lesions in the lungs. 7. A person with both pulmonary TB and extrapulmonary TB should be classified as having pulmonary TB. 8. Rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (RR-TB) is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains resistant to rifampicin. RR-TB cases are often grouped with multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) cases as MDR/RR-TB and are eligible for treatment with an MDR-TB regimen. 9. Rifampicin-susceptible, isoniazid-resistant TB is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains resistant to isoniazid but susceptible to rifampicin. 10. A serious adverse event is one that can result in death, a life-threatening experience, hospitalization or prolonged hospitalization, persistent or significant disability, or a congenital anomaly. Serious adverse events may also require intervention to prevent such outcomes, including discontinuation of the suspected medication. 11. Severe extrapulmonary TB includes miliary (disseminated) TB or TB meningitis. In children under 15 years, extrapulmonary forms of TB other than lymphadenopathy (e.g., peripheral nodes or isolated mediastinal mass without compression) are considered severe. 12. Following a WHO expert consultation in September 2021, intrathoracic lymph node TB in children is now classified as pulmonary TB. 13. A source case refers to a person with TB disease who infected others in a new setting. This could be the index patient or another unidentified individual. 14. Systematic screening for TB disease involves identifying individuals at risk for TB in a predetermined target group by assessing symptoms and using tests, examinations, or other procedures that can be applied rapidly. For those who screen positive, diagnosis must be confirmed through diagnostic tests and clinical assessments. This term is sometimes used interchangeably with active TB case-finding but should be distinguished from testing for TB infection (e.g., TB skin test or interferon-gamma release assay). 15. The tuberculin skin test (TST) involves intradermal injection of mycobacterial antigens that elicit an immune response (delayed-type hypersensitivity), represented by induration, which is measured in millimeters. TST is used to diagnose TB infection. 16. Tuberculosis (TB) refers to the disease state caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. In this document, it is commonly referred to as TB disease to distinguish it from TB infection. 17. TB infection is defined as a state of persistent immune response to stimulation by Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens without evidence of clinically manifest TB disease. This term replaces the previously used latent TB infection. 18. There is no gold standard test for directly identifying Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection in humans. Most infected individuals show no signs or symptoms of TB but remain at risk for developing TB disease. 19. Tuberculosis preventive treatment (TPT) is offered to individuals at risk of TB disease to reduce that risk. It is also referred to as treatment of TB infection or TB preventive therapy. 20. Among children under 10 years, malnutrition is often defined as a weight-for-age Z-score below -2 standard deviations. 21. The WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis, Module 5: Management of tuberculosis in children and adolescents (2022), provide evidence-based recommendations for the care cascade in children and adolescents, aiming to prevent TB, improve case detection and treatment outcomes, and reduce TB-related morbidity and mortality in line with global targets. 22. The guidelines target national TB programs, primary healthcare programs, maternal and child health programs, national AIDS programs, pediatricians, clinicians, and health practitioners working on TB, HIV, and infectious diseases, as well as community-based organizations and implementing partners. 23. The 2022 guidelines include eight new recommendations on TB management in children and adolescents, covering diagnostic approaches, treatment regimens, and models of care. 24. For children with signs and symptoms of pulmonary TB, Xpert Ultra should be used as the initial diagnostic test for TB and rifampicin resistance detection on sputum, nasopharyngeal aspirate, gastric aspirate, or stool, rather than smear microscopy, culture, or phenotypic drug susceptibility testing. 25. Integrated treatment decision algorithms may be used to diagnose pulmonary TB in children with presumptive TB attending healthcare facilities. 26. A four-month treatment regimen is recommended for children and adolescents aged 3 months to 16 years with non-severe TB, without suspicion or evidence of MDR/RR-TB. 27. An all-oral treatment regimen containing bedaquiline may be used for children under six years with MDR/RR-TB. 28. Delamanid may be included in longer regimens for children under three years with MDR/RR-TB. 29. A six-month intensive regimen may be used as an alternative to the 12-month regimen for children with bacteriologically confirmed or clinically diagnosed TB meningitis, without suspicion or evidence of MDR/RR-TB. 30. Decentralized TB services may be used in high TB burden settings for children and adolescents with TB symptoms or exposure. 31. Family-centered, integrated services may complement standard TB services for children and adolescents with TB symptoms or exposure.
